4938.dq: Due to logistical constraints related to travel in Arunachal Pradesh, no time was able to be spent discussing topics such as intonation or sandhi. Instead, I am only able to give a basic overview of the tonemes here.
4938.dloc: van Dam: Section 9.2.4 'Tone Categories', p. 241; toneless-prefix sentence sec. 9.2.4, p. 243; group-level presyllable remark sec. 5.1.3, p. 94; Fig. 7.9 caption, sec. 7.2 Khălak (ch. 7 Southern Rangpang Tangsa), p. 188. Sudhakaran: ch. 1, sec. 1.2.4 'Tutsa Tones', p. 12 (chapter-1 p. 12), Table 1.3.
4938.prule: No word-stress rule stated. Tutsa is described as a lexical tone language: van Dam gives four tonemes on the (monosyllabic) stem syllable (1 mid falling breathy, 2 high level, 3 mid/low falling, 4 checked/short with oral or glottal stop coda); Sudhakaran gives two tones (high vs low) with seven minimal pairs. Sesquisyllabic prefixes (/e0/, /a0/, /ə/) are toneless minor syllables, and for the Tangsa-Nocte group generally 'toneless and unstressed'.
4938.quote: [van Dam p. 241] Figure 9.2 shows the main features of the first three tone categories in Tutsa. Fourth tone is a checked tone, with short duration relative to other tonemes, and an oral or glottal stop coda. What follows is a very early preliminary description. A number of segmental combinations have not been adequately recorded, and nothing has been recorded within carrier sentences. Contours in Tutsa differ considerably from many other Tangsa-Nocte varieties. [...] It is still a four-tone system and the etyma fall under the same category as with other Tangsa-Nocte varieties discussed here.…

4938.tone: Both reachable primaries treat Tutsa as a lexical tone language and say nothing about word stress or accent. van Dam (2023, sec. 9.2): four-tone system on stem syllables, citation forms only, no carrier sentences, intonation and sandhi not studied; the only prominence remarks are group-level, not Tutsa-specific (sec. 5.1.3, p. 94 / p. 112: the presyllable is 'toneless and unstressed'; Fig. 7.9 caption, p. 188 / p. 206, in the Khălak section 7.2 of ch. 7 Southern Rangpang Tangsa: sesquisyllabic prefixes 'are common in Tibeto-Burman and are unstressed and atonal'), i.e. the tone-bearing major syllable is the prominent one and minor syllables are not. Sudhakaran (Tezpur PhD, ch. 1 sec. 1.2.4, p. 12): two tones, high and low, Table 1.3; no stress remark in ch. 1-3 (the only phonology is ch. 1 sec. 1.2). The two sources disagree on the tone inventory (4 vs 2), not on stress.

tn.translation: Stress in Ulch, as in Nanai or Udihe, is expiratory-musical: a weak expiratory stress falls on the vowel of the first syllable, a tonic (or musical) one on the vowel of the last syllable. The vowel of the first syllable is articulated most distinctly. The vowel of the last syllable, on the contrary, is articulated indistinctly, but with a certain, sometimes barely noticeable, rise in pitch. 4954.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the root (right-aligned moraic trochee, rightmost stress rule) in seven of the eight root shapes of Table 3: initial in consonant-initial and long-vowel-initial bisyllables (katha /ˈkat̪a/, uuku /ˈuːku/, ngaani /ˈŋaːni/), second syllable in all trisyllables regardless of onset or vowel length (koloyi /kɔˈlɔji/, ilantyi /iˈlaɲci/, aaliman /ˌaːˈliman/). The one systematic departure (pattern 1, about 9% of roots): bisyllabic roots beginning with a short onsetless vowel take final stress (ikan /iˈkan/), analysed as an unfooted extra-light initial plus a degenerate foot. Vowel length occurs only in the first syllable. Stress is morphologically insensitive.

4959.dq: The preterite is formed with the unstressed prefix be- (if the stem is plain) and the following endings: -im, -i, -/a (m. and f.), -imān, -iān, -an. The stress is placed on the last syllable of the stem. (The source never uses the phrase 'word stress'; all its statements locate stress on prefix, stem or ending within the inflected word, and the fn. 7 convention marks stress on single words.)
4959.dloc: §23 Past-stem intransitive tenses and moods, p. 463; transcription convention fn. 7, p. 454
4959.prule: Stress is called 'functional and predictable' but no positional rule for the word as such is stated; every explicit statement ties stress to morpheme identity: inflectional suffixes are either unstressed (feminine -a, §4 p. 455; fem. sg. dir. -a, masc. sg. obl. -e and pl. dir. -e, all glossed '(unstressed)' in the table of §8 p. 456; preterite/imperfect endings; Gandomābādi imperfect -ay) or stressed (fem. sg. obl. -é and pl. obl. -ā́n in the same table, p. 456; sg. obl. -é(y) and pl. dir. -é on nouns in -á, §10 p. 457, whose pl. obl. -iān is printed without an accent; the present personal endings, 'all of which are stressed', p. 462; the perfect's 'stressed e', p. 463; Gandomābādi perfect -áy, p. 464); verbal prefixes be-/mi- are unstressed in preterite, imperfect and present, while in the subjunctive the prefix bé- carries the stress (bé-gen-em vs present mi-gen-ém, p. 462); in the preterite 'the stress is placed on the last syllable of the stem' (p. 463). A Persian-type default (stress on the last syllable of the stem, so that nouns with the unstressed feminine -a are penultimate: déta, asífa, galína, beside stem-final xondāná) is inferable from fn. 7 ('a final a or e is to be assumed unstressed, unless otherwise marked') and the accented examples, but it is not stated as a rule.

4961.prule: One primary (high) stress per noun or verb word; its position is set morphologically, not by syllable count or weight: by default on the first vowel of the root, but lexically specified affixes (e.g. inchoative -aw-, slow-reduplication -aC) take the high stress and reduce the stem to low (or occasionally secondary) stress; after a weak (schwa) root a word-final monoconsonantal grammatical suffix (-m, -c, -n) is included in the stress domain so that stress falls on the schwa between root and suffix rather than on the root schwa (the consonantal suffix itself cannot bear stress); stress falls in different places in the perfective and imperfective aspect forms of one root (Kinkade 1993: 183). Compounds carry one primary stress.
4961.srule: Secondary stress reported, placement not given: Kinkade 1963 (sec. 1.1.2) distinguishes high (primary), secondary and low stress phonemes; 'Compound and reduplicated stems frequently have a high and a secondary stress, but the order in which they occur is variable. Secondary stress is not as common as high stress'; a stem whose affix takes the high stress is 'reduced to low, or occasionally secondary, stress'. No rhythmic or positional rule. Rowicka 2000: 113-114 instead describes Upper Chehalis as a system 'where only primary stress is manifested'.

4962.dloc: Preprint sec. 1 'Introduction' p. 2 ('lexical stress... Guinea-Bissau Kriyol') with fn. 2 (pp. 2-3); sec. 2 p. 12, rule (15) ('periphery of the phonological word'); published pp. 97-109.
4962.heavy: A heavy syllable is one that has a realized coda, and the list of possible codas appears to be the same in K and S and in Portuguese, viz. sonorants and approximants (/l/, /r/, /N/, /I/, /U/) and /s/ [p. 3]; plural /-s/ does not count [p. 11]; for rule (15) the authors add 'left-heavy' syllables made heavy by a branching onset (N + prenasalized consonant), which count only at the left edge of the phonological word, versus 'right-heavy' (coda) syllables, which count only at the right edge [p. 12].
4962.prule: Nouns: stress the penultimate syllable unless the final syllable is heavy, i.e. has a realized coda (/l/, /r/, /N/, glides /I/ /U/, /s/ - but not the plural suffix -s), in which case the final syllable is stressed (plánta, minjér, kabás vs kásas). Verbs: final stress irrespective of syllable structure (plantá, kumé, bambú).
4962.srule: Not mentioned in Andrade & Kihm 2000 (preprint pp. 1-17 read). Kihm & Laks 1989 (instrumental, one Bissau speaker): secondary stresses are optional 'echoes' whose position follows from the main stress -- in nouns/adjectives of three or more syllables a possible but non-regular echo on the initial syllable (àplikasón, pùrgisúzu); in polysyllabic verbs (initial main stress in their analysis) an echo of variable strength on the final syllable. Bull 1989 p. 77 (second-hand via Chapouto 2014 p. 17): trisyllabic final-stressed nouns and numerals of more than three syllables carry a secondary stress on the first syllable.
4962.quote: This suggests a very simple rule, for all intents and purposes identical with that which seems to hold in Portuguese, namely: assign stress to the penultimate syllable, unless the ultimate syllable is heavy, in which case it bears stress. A heavy syllable is one that has a realized coda, and the list of possible codas appears to be the same in K and S and in Portuguese, viz. sonorants and approximants (/l/, /r/, /N/, /I/, /U/) and /s/. [p. 5] ... plural /-s/ as opposed to base-internal final /s/ does not make the syllable it attaches to heavy in the relevant sense (compare kásas ‘houses’ and kabás ‘calabash’). [p. 11] ... More …
4962.tone: Andrade & Kihm treat Kriyol as a stress language and abstract away from the phonetic realization (fn. 2, referring to 'Kihm & Laks 1990, L'accent en kriyol, Linx' = Kihm & Laks 1989, De l'accent en kriyol, Linx 20: 89-111, an instrumental study (duration, pitch and intensity measured per syllable, one Bissau speaker) which concludes that Kriyol is a stress language, 'le kriyol est bien une langue à accent': one maximally prominent syllable per accentual unit, with secondary 'echo' stresses in longer words). Chapouto 2014 p. 17 reports Couto 1994 as concluding that a tonal contour is evident in traditional creole, with stress more patent in the lusitanised variety; Bull 1989, Andrade et al. 1992 and Kihm 1994 all treat it as accentual. The Frontiers 2021 creole-prosody survey lists Guinea-Bissau Kriyol as analysed as stress, not tone.

tn.quote: dans un système de type accentuel, une et une seule syllabe par domaine accentuable présente une proéminence absolue. ... De ce point de vue, le kriyol est bien une langue à accent. Toute unité accentuable ... présente une et une seule syllabe maximalement proéminente. ... la proéminence syllabique ne possède pas de corrélats absolus: elle peut se traduire par une augmentation de l'intensité, de la longueur, de la hauteur ou toute combinaison possible de ces facteurs. Il en est ainsi en kriyol.
tn.translation: in an accentual-type system, one and only one syllable per accentual domain shows an absolute prominence. ... From this point of view, Kriyol is indeed an accent language. Every accentual unit ... shows one and only one maximally prominent syllable. ... syllabic prominence has no absolute correlates: it may be expressed by an increase in intensity, length, pitch, or any combination of these factors. So it is in Kriyol.
